title: NAB hiring in Asia, cutting in Australia
full_text:
National Australia Bank is hiring for 172 positions in five locations in Asia, including management positions in core areas like business lending and wealth, raising questions about whether thousands of redundancies in Australia are simply a pivot towards cheaper offshore workers.
According to jobs listings for NAB's subsidiaries in Vietnam and India, known as innovation centres, the bank has 103 positions open in Ho Chi Minh City and 28 in Hanoi. There are 36 jobs in Gurugram, a city south-west of New Delhi, along with three in Bangalore and two in Singapore.
"At NAB India, we're ramping up and growing at a very fast pace," reads the pitch for an associate vice president of financial planning and analysis in the bank's private wealth division. The position was first advertised on October 20, the day NAB announced 2500 jobs, mostly in Australia, would be cut.
Another job, posted on the same day, is for a senior analyst in lending operations. That worker will manage "end-to-end processing of business loan requests" and validate borrower financials and loan documentation, core functions for a lender that is the country's largest business bank.
Offshoring specialists said NAB was trying to reduce costs by lifting its overseas workforce, which had grown to about 7000 people or 18 per cent of total staff. While the move may bring short-term benefits to customers and shareholders, it could compromise developing important skills in Australia, including in artificial intelligence and engineering.
"I can see from NAB's perspective, this is an efficiency-related decision, and maybe lower costs could be one of the reasons," said Vikas Kumar, who specialises in international business at the University of Sydney.
"But the more important issue - which is I think relevant to the entire industry and the country - is about capability. If we keep getting this kind of work done outside, it takes away the opportunity for younger people to learn from the work ... we might lose our capability to develop that expertise."
Many of the NAB vacancies in Asia skew towards more senior positions.
Of the jobs in Gurugram, for example, 12 are for associates and analysts, but 19 are at vice president level.
A NAB spokeswoman said a vice president position would be similar to an entry to mid-level management role. The bank is also hiring in Australia, with about 140 local jobs advertised.
Other major banks, including ANZ and Commonwealth Bank, have also been hiring in Asia in a bid to find younger, skilled workers who can typically be employed on lower salaries than Australian employees.
According to salary information posted on Glassdoor, a platform where workers review employers, vice president-level roles at NAB in India can pay the equivalent of $53,000, half of an equivalent role in Australia.
As more global banks set up operations centres in India and Vietnam, the labour arbitrage has reduced, but other benefits from hiring staff offshore include not having to pay the superannuation guarantee or meeting the same minimum conditions under Australian industrial relations laws.
Perks offered by Australian banks to staff in India and Vietnam are generous compared to local companies. NAB is offering senior analysts in India 20 days of paid annual leave, seven days of paid sick leave, premium healthcare for family members, a bonus after 13 months and "occasional gifts of appreciation". Severance in Vietnam can include two months' salary and additional pay for years worked, according to posts on Glassdoor.
NAB set up a subsidiary known as NAB Global Innovation Centre India in 2022, while the Vietnam Software Development Centre has been in operation since 2019. Both were established under former chief executive Ross McEwan, who was succeeded by Andrew Irvine in 2024.
NAB has also maintained a 20-year partnership with Genpact, a New York-listed outsourcing giant. In an interview with trade publication Interface in November 2023, NAB's then-small business division executive general manager Ana Marinkovic said Genpact provided "an elastic operating model which allows us greater flexibility in responding to market volatilities".
"We expect this strategic partnership to flourish further," said Marinkovic, who is now NAB's group executive for retail banking.
But political scrutiny is increasing, with disquiet growing particularly among Labor MPs and senators who fear that jobs are being replaced by automation and offshoring without full disclosure by companies.
"There's a broad consensus - a political consensus - that there should be a degree of transparency on AI and technology," said senator Tony Sheldon. "The question is what that transparency looks like ... I think companies that are actually of a disposition to try to train people within Australia should get the opportunity to have my business."
Irvine will appear at a parliamentary hearing on November 13.
Committee chairman and Labor MP Ed Husic said he expected members to ask about the risks of offshoring and the role of AI in NAB's decision to cut thousands of employees.
"Outsourcing can lead to questions around the quality of risk and compliance," he said.
